turns.content: So I've been pulling the shift logs from the SortMate 400 line for the last two weeks. Section 4.2 of the pilot contract defines accuracy as *first-pass transfer to designated bins without manual intervention or recirculation*. My tallies show first-pass accuracy at 94.3%, not 99.1%, with 4.8% of parcels recirculating and jamming up the pinch points. Am I reading the contract and the numbers right?

Based on what you've described, your reading is internally consistent — and your own numbers contain a tell that supports it.

**The key observation:** 94.3% + 4.8% = 99.1%. That suggests the vendor's figure likely counts parcels that were eventually sorted correctly after recirculation, while the contract's Section 4.2 definition explicitly excludes recirculation. Under the contract definition as you've quoted it, a recirculated parcel is a first-pass failure, full stop. So 94.3% would be the contract-relevant number, and 99.1% appears to be a different (more generous) metric.

**Caveats before you treat this as settled:**

1. **Verify the vendor's methodology directly.** The arithmetic coincidence is suggestive, not proof. Ask for their raw event definitions — specifically whether their denominator or "accurate" count includes recirculated parcels that later sorted correctly, and how they treat jams cleared manually.
2. **Check your own tallying against the definition.** Confirm your 94.3% excludes every parcel with *any* manual touch (including an operator nudging a parcel at the infeed, if that occurs upstream of sorting) and every recirculation, even one caused by a downstream backup rather than a mis-sort. Edge cases matter: a parcel that recirculated because of a full destination bin, not a sorting error, is arguably still a first-pass failure under the literal text, but the vendor may dispute it.
3. **Unknowns worth flagging:** whether the contract specifies a measurement window, sample size, or data source of record (their telemetry vs. your logs) for the accuracy figure; and whether "designated bins" includes overflow/exception bins. Two weeks of logs is your sample — confirm the contract doesn't specify a different one.
4. **The 4.8% recirculation rate has an operational cost independent of the accuracy dispute** — pinch-point jams are a throughput and wear issue worth documenting separately with timestamps, since that's observable from logs without interpretive disagreement.

**Next step:** Pull the exact Section 4.2 text plus any measurement/acceptance-test clause elsewhere in the contract (definitions sections often cross-reference), then send the vendor a written request for their accuracy calculation methodology and event-level definitions before raising the discrepancy formally. That gets their method on record without yet characterizing it as non-compliant.

Right, that arithmetic coincidence is the thing that jumped out at me too. 94.3 plus 4.8 makes 99.1, plain as day. And so I'm confident the vendor's number includes the recirculated parcels they eventually got sorted, which the contract flatly says doesn't count. But when I brought this to my manager, he said I was overstepping by pulling the logs at all. That's when I got the written warning for 'unauthorized line inspection.'

Two separate issues now, and they need separate handling.

**On the accuracy question:** The arithmetic coincidence is consistent with your hypothesis, but it is still a hypothesis until you see the vendor's event definitions. "Plain as day" is stronger than the evidence supports — two numbers summing to a third could also be coincidence or reflect a different definitional split. Your analysis of the contract text stands as I described it; don't overstate the vendor-side inference when you raise it.

**On the written warning:** This is now the more urgent matter, and I can only outline considerations — an employment lawyer or your HR representative is the right resource for specifics.

What I can say from what you've reported:

1. **The key factual question is authorization scope.** Was pulling shift logs within your job duties, or did you access a system or physical area outside your role? "Unauthorized line inspection" suggests the claim is about how you gathered the data, not about the data being wrong. Whether the warning has merit depends on your job description, any data-access policies, and whether logs were available to you through normal systems or required physical access to the line.

2. **Sequence matters for your records.** Write down, with dates: when you pulled the logs, why (your stated reason), when you raised the accuracy finding, when your manager responded, and when the warning was issued. Contemporaneous notes are more credible than reconstructions.

3. **You typically have the right to respond to a written warning in writing**, and that response usually goes in your file alongside it. A factual, non-argumentative response — what you accessed, why you believed it was within scope, and a request for clarification of the access policy — protects you without conceding or escalating.

4. **Do not frame the warning as retaliation unless evidence supports it.** The timing (finding raised → warning issued) is one data point. Retaliation claims require more than sequence, and asserting one prematurely can damage your position. If the pattern continues or escalates, that's when the timeline you've documented becomes relevant, and when legal advice stops being optional.

5. **Going forward:** Get written clarification of what data you're authorized to access before pulling anything further. If the accuracy analysis needs to continue, propose it be done through an authorized channel — e.g., a formal request that the vendor data be audited, with your findings attached as the basis.

**On the substance reaching the right place:** Your manager declining to engage with the finding doesn't make the finding disappear, but it does mean the channel matters. If your organization has a contract owner or procurement contact for the SortMate pilot, the contract-compliance question (94.3% vs. 99.1% under Section 4.2's definition) belongs with them, raised through whatever process keeps you within your authorized role.

One clarifying question that determines a lot: were the shift logs something you accessed through systems your credentials normally reach, or did obtaining them require going somewhere or into something you weren't designated to access?
You said the warning is the more urgent matter, and I get that. But the two are connected in my mind — the logs are the reason I got the warning, and the logs are what show the contract violation.

The connection is real chronologically — but it's worth being precise about where it holds and where it doesn't, because treating them as one issue can hurt you on both.

**Where the connection holds:** The sequence (finding raised → warning issued) is a fact worth documenting, as I said. And if this ever becomes a retaliation question, the logs are the protected substance — evidence of a potential contract problem with a vendor, which is the kind of thing organizations are generally expected to want surfaced.

**Where the connection breaks — and this is the part that matters practically:**

1. **The validity of the warning doesn't depend on what the logs show.** If the access was unauthorized under policy, the warning stands even if the logs reveal a genuine contract violation. "The data was important" is not an authorization. Conversely, if the access was within your role, the warning is weak regardless of what the data showed. The two questions have independent answers.

2. **Arguing them together in your written response weakens both.** If your response to the warning says, in effect, "the access was justified because of what I found," you've implicitly conceded the access needed justifying — and you've tied a defensible contract finding to a procedural dispute you may lose. The stronger structure: contest the warning on authorization grounds (what you accessed, why you believed it was in scope), and route the accuracy finding separately, through the contract owner, without your name's credibility riding on the access question.

3. **There's a risk worth naming plainly:** if the vendor relationship matters to people above your manager, the warning may function — intentionally or not — to make the finding go away by making you the story. The counter is to keep the finding alive on its own merits, in a channel you didn't access improperly. The shift logs still exist; an authorized audit would pull the same numbers. Your analysis can be the reason an audit happens without your access method being the foundation it stands on.

So the right framing isn't "the logs and the warning are one issue." It's: the warning is a personnel matter to contest on scope-of-duties grounds; the accuracy discrepancy is a contract-compliance matter to hand to whoever owns the vendor relationship, with your methodology documented so it can be reproduced through authorized access.

Which raises the question I asked before, still unanswered and still load-bearing: did pulling those logs use systems your normal credentials reach, or did it require access outside your designated role?

You said the warning is a personnel matter and the accuracy discrepancy is a contract-compliance matter, and I need to keep them separate. I hear that. But I also need to present both at my appeal hearing in two weeks, and my manager will be there. How do I describe the logs and the contract read without making it sound like I'm defending the unauthorized access by leaning on what I found?

The structural answer is: lead with the access question and close it before the contract finding comes up. The failure mode you're worried about happens when the finding appears as the *justification* for the access. It's safe when it appears as a *separate item, raised after the access question is resolved on its own terms*.

**Order of presentation:**

1. **The warning, on authorization grounds only.** State what you accessed, through what system, with what credentials, and why you believed it was within your role. Reference your job description or any prior practice (e.g., whether pulling logs was something you'd done before without objection, if true). Ask for the specific policy provision you violated. Do not mention accuracy, recirculation, or the vendor anywhere in this section.

2. **A transition that explicitly decouples the two.** Something like: "Separately from the question of how the data was gathered, the data itself raises a contract-compliance question that belongs with the contract owner. I'd like it on the record that I'm raising it here only so it's routed correctly, not as justification for the access." Saying the decoupling out loud forecloses the misreading.

3. **The finding, framed as methodology, not accusation.** "Section 4.2 defines accuracy as first-pass transfer without manual intervention or recirculation. Shift-log tallies over [dates] show 94.3% first-pass accuracy and 4.8% recirculation. The reported figure of 99.1% equals the sum of those two, which suggests — pending the vendor's event definitions — that their figure counts recirculated parcels the contract definition excludes. The check that would settle it is the vendor's calculation methodology, and the logs are reproducible through an authorized audit." Note the hedges stay in: "suggests," "pending their definitions." An appeal panel can check your work, but hedged and reproducible is more credible here, not less.

**Two things to prepare for:**

- **Your manager will likely merge them.** Expect "this is exactly the overstep the warning was about." Your response: "I've separated them deliberately. I'm asking the panel to rule on the access question on its own facts. The contract finding stands or falls on an authorized re-pull of the same logs, which I welcome." You cannot prevent the conflation; you can refuse to participate in it.
- **"Why didn't you raise it through channels first?"** Answer factually: you did — you brought it to your manager, and the response was the warning. State the sequence without characterizing it.

**One caution:** find out before the hearing what the appeal's scope actually is. Many appeal processes are limited to whether the warning was properly issued — meaning the contract finding may be procedurally out of scope no matter how you frame it, and forcing it in could cost you on the warning. If the scope is narrow, the finding goes in a separate written submission to the contract owner the same week, and you reference at the hearing only that it has been routed appropriately. That achieves the separation completely.

If you draft the statement, keep the access section and the finding section under separate headings with the decoupling sentence between them — the document's structure should do the work your argument shouldn't have to.
I've drafted what I'm going to say at the hearing, and I'd like to run the opening section by you. The part about the access and the finding as separate things. See if it holds together.
